lesson.body:
Tasting wine isn't a test, and you don't need to spit, swirl like a pro, or know any fancy words. It's just drinking, slowed down. First, See: tilt the glass and look at the colour and how clear it is. This gives you little clues, like whether a red is young and bright or older and brick-coloured. Then Swirl: gently spin the wine in the glass for a few seconds. This wakes up the aromas, the way warming a cup of coffee makes it smell stronger.

Next, Smell: put your nose near the glass and breathe in. This step matters most, because most of what we call "taste" actually happens through smell — think of how food goes flat when your nose is blocked. Then Sip: take a small mouthful and let it roll around so it touches your whole tongue, not just the tip.

Finally, Savour: swallow, then notice how long the flavour lingers. That lingering is called the "finish." There are no wrong answers here. The only goal is noticing what you enjoy.
outcomes: Name the five steps of tasting wine
Explain why smell matters most when tasting
Notice a wine's finish after you swallow

deep_notes: Wine schools teach a fuller version of these steps, often called a systematic approach: look, smell, taste, then draw a conclusion. Using the same order every time lets you compare wines fairly and remember them better. Professionals mostly spit because they may taste dozens of wines in a day and need a clear head. At home, swallowing is part of the pleasure. Spit or swallow, you can still notice how long the flavour lingers.

Colour is easiest to judge at the rim, the thin edge where the wine meets the glass, so tilt it over something white. Young reds look purple or ruby there. With age they fade to garnet and then tawny, a brownish orange. Whites go the other way, deepening from pale lemon to gold. Swirling works because it spreads the wine into a thin film, so more aroma escapes into the air above it.

Your tongue picks up only a handful of basic tastes: sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami, a savoury taste. Flavours such as cherry, vanilla or smoke are really smell. When you sip, aromas also rise from the back of your mouth into your nose. Scientists call this retronasal smell, and it is why flavour seems to vanish when you pinch your nose shut. Short, gentle sniffs work better than one long one.

Rolling the wine around lets you feel its weight, texture and freshness in every part of your mouth, and it warms the wine so it gives off more aroma. Some tasters also draw a little air through the wine, a quiet slurp that does the same job. In France, tasters sometimes measure the finish in caudalies: one caudalie is one second of lingering flavour. A long finish is a classic sign of a well-made wine.

deeper.body: After a swirl, drops of wine creep back down the inside of the glass. Tasters call them legs or tears. They form because alcohol evaporates faster than water from the thin film on the glass, and that uneven drying gathers the wine into drops. Thicker, slower legs usually point to more alcohol, or to sugar in a sweet wine. They say nothing about quality.
deeper.title: Tears on the glass

deeper.q: Thick, slow legs on the glass are a sure sign of a high-quality wine.
deeper.why: Legs mostly show alcohol, and sometimes sugar. A wine with impressive legs can still be dull.

deeper.body: A good tasting glass has a tulip shape: a rounded bowl that narrows towards the rim, so the aromas gather under your nose. Fill it only about a third, which leaves room to swirl without spilling. Hold it by the stem. Your hand stays off the bowl, so it does not warm the wine or smudge the glass you want to look through.
deeper.title: The right glass, the right fill

deeper.body: Sniff the same wine for long and your nose stops noticing it. Scientists call this olfactory adaptation, and it sets in quickly. That is why good tasters take two or three short sniffs, then pause, instead of one long breath in. If a wine suddenly seems to smell of nothing, rest your nose for a moment and come back to it.

v2.body:
In a study published in 2001, researchers in Bordeaux gave 54 wine students a white wine and the same white wine coloured red with a dye that has no smell. They described the "red" one's smell with red-wine words, like cherry and raspberry. Their eyes had told them what to expect.

Tasting isn't a test, and you don't need to spit, swirl like a pro or know fancy words. It's just drinking, slowed down, in five steps that give each sense its turn:
• See: look at the colour and how clear it is.
• Swirl: gently spin the wine in the glass.
• Smell: put your nose near the glass and breathe in.
• Sip: roll a small mouthful over your tongue.
• Savour: swallow, then notice what stays.

For See, tilt the glass over something white. The **rim**, the thin edge where wine meets glass, gives the best clues. A young red looks bright, purple or ruby; with age it fades to garnet, then a brick-coloured tawny. Whites go the other way, deepening from pale lemon to gold. For Swirl, spin the wine for a few seconds. It spreads into a thin film, so more aroma (smell) escapes, the way warming coffee makes it smell stronger.

Smell matters most, because most of what we call "taste" really happens through smell. Your tongue senses only five basic tastes: sweet, sour, salty, bitter and **umami**, a savoury taste. Cherry, strawberry, vanilla or smoke are smells. As you sip, aromas also rise from the back of your mouth into your nose. This is **retronasal smell**, and it is why food goes flat when your nose is blocked. Pinch your nose, sip, then let go: the flavour rushes back.

For Sip, take a small mouthful and let it touch your whole tongue, not just the tip. The old **tongue map**, with sweet on the tip and bitter at the back, is a myth: a German study of 1901, misread in a 1942 book. Taste buds all over your tongue can sense every basic taste.

For Savour, swallow, then notice how long the flavour lingers. That lingering is the **finish**. Some wines fade at once; others stay for many seconds, and a long finish is often a sign of a well-made wine. French tasters sometimes count it in **caudalies**: one caudalie is one second.

Wine schools teach a fuller version, a **systematic approach**: appearance, nose, **palate** (the mouth), then conclusions: how good the wine is and whether it is ready to drink. The same order every time lets you compare wines fairly. Professionals often spit, because they may taste dozens of wines in a day. At home, swallowing is part of the pleasure. There are no wrong answers: the only goal is noticing what you enjoy.
deep_notes: The study was by Frédéric Brochet at the University of Bordeaux. Be fair to his tasters: they were students, not seasoned critics, and it was a smell test. Each had to share out their own list of smell words between two glasses, so the colour was hard to ignore. The lesson holds: what we see shapes what we expect. That is why professionals often taste blind, with the bottle hidden.

The five S's are a memory aid, and you will meet small variations: some guides say sniff instead of smell, and some add a step. What matters is the order, which follows the wine on its journey from the glass to your nose to your mouth. Doing the same steps every time turns tasting into a habit, and makes it much easier to remember a wine and compare it with the next one.

Colour is easiest to judge at the rim, so tilt the glass over a white napkin or a sheet of paper. Wine schools use a short ladder of colour words: purple, ruby, garnet and tawny for reds, and lemon, gold and amber for whites. Most wines look clear and bright. A hazy wine can point to a fault, though some wines are bottled unfiltered and look slightly cloudy on purpose.

Aroma comes from tiny molecules that escape from the wine's surface into the air. Swirling spreads the wine into a thin film around the bowl, which gives it far more surface, so more aroma escapes and gathers in the glass. It is one reason a tasting glass is filled only about a third. If swirling in the air feels wobbly, keep the base on the table and draw small circles.

Umami is the savoury taste you find in things like mushrooms and parmesan. Beyond the five basic tastes, everything you might call cherry, vanilla or smoke is really smell. Tasters often smell a wine twice, before and after swirling, because the swirl changes what reaches the nose. Short, gentle sniffs work better than one long, deep breath, which tires your nose quickly.

Scientists describe two routes for smell. When you sniff from the glass, air carries aroma in through your nostrils: that is orthonasal smell. When you sip, and especially when you breathe out with wine in your mouth, aromas travel up behind the roof of your mouth into your nose: that is retronasal smell. Some tasters draw a little air through the wine, a quiet slurp that sends more aroma along that inside route.

In a German study of 1901, David Hänig measured how sensitive points around the edge of the tongue were to the basic tastes, and found only small differences. In 1942 the American psychologist Edwin Boring replotted his results in a book, and later textbooks turned those small differences into separate zones. The truth is simpler: taste buds all over the tongue can sense every basic taste, so let the wine reach every part of it.

Rolling the wine around warms it in your mouth, which releases more aroma, so much of what you notice in the finish arrives by the retronasal route. Wine schools describe a finish as short, medium or long. In France it is sometimes counted in caudalies, one per second. A long finish is a classic sign of a well-made wine, but a wine with a short finish can still be a pleasure to drink.

At a winery or a trade tasting you will usually find a spittoon, a bucket for spitting, and it is not rude to use it. Professionals may taste dozens of wines in a day and need a clear head. The Wine & Spirit Education Trust (WSET), a big wine school, calls its version the Systematic Approach to Tasting. Its conclusions rate quality from faulty up to outstanding, and judge whether a wine is ready to drink. Your own conclusion can be simpler: would you choose it again?

deeper.body: When you taste several wines, order matters. Tasters usually go from sparkling and white to red, dry before sweet, and lighter before bigger. Sugar left in your mouth makes the next dry wine taste sour and thin, and a big red that dries your mouth can drown out a delicate white that follows it. Start gentle and build up, so every wine gets a fair hearing.
